pattern: Myth vs fact carousel, remade from the 'just let them cry it out' debunk format seen in separation anxiety training content
why: Naming a common piece of advice owners have already heard, then calmly correcting it, makes the right person swipe to see what to do instead.

slides.headline: Your dog cries the second you leave?
body: You're not a bad owner. Swipe.

image.prompt: Candid iPhone photo of a medium-sized beagle mix lying calmly on a doormat inside a small city flat hallway, looking up at the closed front door, keys hanging on a hook, soft natural morning light from a side window, warm muted tones, dog relaxed and not distressed, lower third of frame plain wooden floor, no text, no logos

slides.headline: Myth: just let them cry it out
body: Pushing too far, too fast can make alone time feel scarier.

image.prompt: Candid iPhone photo in a bright city flat hallway, a young adult putting on a coat while a calm terrier mix sits on the floor watching them, natural daylight, relaxed atmosphere, soft focus background, lower part of frame simple floorboards, no text, no logos, no screens

slides.headline: Fact: calm alone time is built in small steps
body: Hound builds a daily plan for your dog's age and problem.

image.prompt: Photoreal cosy living room in a city flat, a dog curled up asleep on a soft rug near a sofa, warm afternoon window light, plants on a shelf, calm and uncluttered, no text, no logos

slides.headline: Myth: you need hours a day to train
body: One short exercise a day, about 10 minutes.

image.prompt: Candid iPhone photo of a person in their thirties sitting cross-legged on a living room floor, gently offering a treat to an attentive spaniel mix sitting in front of them, soft morning light through a window, relaxed and happy mood, plain rug in the lower third, no text, no logos, no screens

slides.headline: Fact: tiny wins are real progress
body: Streaks help you see your practice adding up.
Really struggling? A vet or behaviourist can help.

image.prompt: Candid iPhone photo of a relaxed dog lying on a round rug happily chewing a red rubber chew toy, owner's legs visible on a sofa in the background slightly out of focus, warm natural light, calm home setting, lower third of frame simple rug texture, no text, no logos

slides.headline: Start with the quick quiz for your dog
body: Puppy, adolescent, adult or senior. Begin there.

image.prompt: Candid iPhone photo of a dog peacefully asleep on a soft blanket on a sofa in a sunlit city flat, gentle golden afternoon light, calm and quiet mood, plain softly lit wall in the upper third, no text, no logos, no people

caption: Letting them cry it out isn't the shortcut it sounds like. Calm alone time is practised in small, doable steps, about 10 minutes a day. Take the quiz to get a plan built for your dog's age, and if your dog is really struggling when left, please speak to a vet or qualified behaviourist.

findings.message: Five of the six slides use AI-generated photoreal images, including people on slides 2 and 4, so apply the TikTok or Meta AI-generated content label at posting time per the pack checklist.
findings.excerpt: image: generated prompt: Candid iPhone photo

slides.issues: Strong, relatable hook and a believable hallway scene. The beagle looks calm and attentive rather than distressed, so the image slightly undersells 'cries'. Headline sits on a good dark gradient and reads well at phone size. The 'Swipe' subline is small but fine.

The owner putting on a coat while the dog watches tells the story well. The cropped head reads as candid, which is fine. The body copy wraps with a lonely orphan word 'scarier.', so tighten the copy or the text box. The dog's face is slightly soft and generic.

The real Hound site is clearly shown on a phone, which passes the product gate. The mockup is a clean render floating on a blurred room, so it reads more like an ad than a creator post. A hand holding the phone would feel more native. There is an orphan word 'problem.' in the body. The on-screen 'behavior' spelling is American against UK copy, which is acceptable because it is the real site, but worth aligning.

The image has a polished stock-photo gloss: even soft lighting, a posed smile and a staged living room. Her skin is a little smooth and the treat hand is borderline. The myth headline is clear and the orange emphasis works.
slides.betterImagePrompt: Candid phone photo of a woman in her thirties in a hoodie kneeling on a kitchen floor, holding a small treat for a springer spaniel that is sitting and looking up at her, a slightly messy UK kitchen behind them, natural window light, mild grain, slightly off-centre framing, realistic hands and fur, no text, no logos

slides.issues: The dog chewing a toy while the owner relaxes is a good 'tiny win' visual. The dog's eyes and the fur texture lean slightly AI, and the composition is very tidy. The two-line body sits on busy carpet texture, so the gradient should be a touch darker. The streaks claim has no app visual to support it.
slides.betterImagePrompt: Candid phone photo of a collie lying on a living room rug calmly chewing a rubber treat toy, an owner's legs in jeans resting on a sofa in the background, afternoon window light, natural fur detail, slight grain, lived-in room, no text, no logos

slides.issues: Clear CTA with the app icon and the houndapp.xyz pill. The sleeping doodle gives a calm payoff to the story. The pill could be slightly larger and higher in contrast. A 'link in bio' cue would help on Instagram.

final.notes: Gate passes: the real Hound site appears on a phone on slide 3, and the CTA with houndapp.xyz is on slide 6. The myth and fact structure is coherent and on-brand, and the vet or behaviourist safety line is good. Suggested fixes: (1) replace the floating phone mockup on slide 3 with a hand-held phone shot so it feels native; (2) reshoot slides 4 and 5 to remove the stock gloss and AI fur and eye tells; (3) fix the orphan words on slides 2 and 3; (4) consider adding a streak screen from the app on slide 5 to make the claim tangible; (5) make the slide 1 dog look more anxious, for example pawing or whining at the door, to strengthen the hook.
